newsitem.title: UK: UK TV ad costs slammed by Procter & Gamble.
newsitem.headline: UK TV ad costs slammed by Procter & Gamble.

text.p: Television advertising costs in Britain are rising so much that advertisers are looking at other ways of attracting consumers, a senior Procter & Gamble executive told a conference organised by the Incorporated Society of British Advertisers (ISBA) on Tuesday.

"Over the last five years TV advertising costs have risen by up to 47 percent and clearly this is unacceptable to business," said Paul Polman vice president and general manager of Procter & Gamble UK & Ireland.

Procter & Gamble is the biggest advertiser in the world with an annual spend estimated at over 3 billion pounds. It is credited with inventing television soap operas -- so called because Procter & Gamble used mini television dramas to advertise its household products to a mass audience in the 1950s.
Polman said that media inflation was fuelled by the fact that the demand for advertising air time out strips supply.
"Because 76 per cent of British homes have a choice of only two commercial channels, the UK is not a truly competitive market," he said.
Polman said that the situation was further exacerbated because the BBC does not carry advertising.
"One of the effects of this arrangement is to put an artificial limit on the UK advertising market which is bad for the economy," he said.
As television advertising costs continued to increase Polman said that he was investigating other ways of communicating with customers such as direct mail.
Polman called for ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5 -- which will be launched this month -- to be allowed to carry more advertising.
The European Union recommends that member countries should allow nine minutes per hour of advertising. ITV Channel 4 and Channel 5 are only allowed to sell 7 minutes per hour on a daily basis.
"If the maximum daily average were to go up to nine minutes that would give TV stations and advertisers more freedom to balance demand and supply," he said.

David Elstein chief executive of Channel 5 told the same conference that "Channel 5 owes its existence to the efforts of advertisers and groups such as ISBA. It is the advertisers not the producers and broadcasters who have pushed hardest for Channel 5."
